item.title: Vanua o Vuda announces passing of Tui Vuda
item.description: The Vanua o Vuda has confirmed the passing of the late Tui Vuda, Ratu Eparama Kitione Tavaiqia, who died on Thursday, July 30. Taukei Nakelo, Ratu Josaia Natakele, said the traditional protocols were observed before the news was made public.
item.content:encoded:
The Vanua o Vuda has confirmed the passing of the late Tui Vuda, Ratu Eparama Kitione Tavaiqia, who died on Thursday, July 30.

Taukei Nakelo, Ratu Josaia Natakele, said the traditional protocols were observed before the news was made public.

He said the Vanua o Vuda first informed all traditional and chiefly houses across Fiji’s 14 provinces, including the President and Tui Cakau, Ratu Naiqama Lalabalavu, before announcing the death publicly.

Ratu Josaia said the Vanua is now preparing for the late paramount chief’s funeral, which is scheduled for August 12.

The late Ratu Eparama was installed as Tui Vuda in February 2011 and served as the traditional leader of the Vanua for more than 15 years.

Traditional preparations for the funeral are now underway as members of the Vanua and visitors prepare to pay their final respects to the late chief.

item.title: Financial inclusion hits record 87%, but many Fijians still struggle to save: RBF Survey
item.description: Formal financial inclusion in Fiji has reached its highest level on record, with 87 per cent of adults now using formal financial services, according to the Reserve Bank of Fiji’s (RBF) 2025 Fiji Financial Services Demand Side Survey. item.content:encoded:
Formal financial inclusion in Fiji has reached its highest level on record, with 87 per cent of adults now using formal financial services, according to the Reserve Bank of Fiji’s (RBF) 2025 Fiji Financial Services Demand Side Survey.

The survey shows significant progress over the past decade, with formal financial inclusion increasing from 64 per cent in 2014, to 81 per cent in 2020, and now 87 per cent in 2025.

The biggest gains have been recorded among people living with disabilities, where formal financial inclusion has risen by 10 percentage points to 91 per cent, and the self-employed, which increased by 14 percentage points to 97 per cent.

Despite the overall improvement, the survey highlights that financial exclusion remains highest among people living in the Northern Division (19 per cent), youths (16 per cent), and rural communities (15 per cent). Encouragingly, formal financial inclusion is now broadly equal between men and women.

However, the survey found that personal bank account ownership has fallen to 68 per cent, despite more people accessing formal financial services. Women (63 per cent), youths (63 per cent), and rural residents (61 per cent) are less likely to own bank accounts, with the gender gap widening to 10 percentage points.

One of the most notable changes has been the rapid adoption of mobile money accounts, which have surged from 7 per cent in 2014 and 17 per cent in 2020 to 67 per cent in 2025. Ownership is highest among people aged 36 to 55 years (77 per cent) and residents of the Central Division (72 per cent). Nearly three-quarters of banked Fijians also use mobile money services.

Digital banking has also become increasingly popular. The use of internet banking among banked customers has increased by 27 percentage points since 2020, with 38 per cent now using online banking services. Uptake is strongest among younger adults, those aged 36 to 55 years, and urban residents.

Insurance coverage, however, has remained unchanged, with only 14 per cent of Fijians holding an insurance policy. Awareness of climate-related insurance has almost doubled to 53 per cent, while adoption has quadrupled to 8 per cent since the previous survey.

The report also found that 74 per cent of Fijians have no outstanding loans or credit, while 10 per cent hold formal loans through financial institutions, mainly commercial banks. Informal borrowing, largely from family and friends, remains common.

Remittances continue to play a vital role in household finances. Forty-two per cent of Fijians receive remittances compared with 21 per cent who send them. Most remittances come from overseas and are transferred through formal channels such as mobile money (72 per cent) and money transfer services (23 per cent).

While access to financial services has improved, the survey paints a more challenging picture of household finances.

Only 39 per cent of respondents said they were always satisfied with their financial situation, while just 24 per cent believed they were on track to achieve their financial goals.

The survey found 33 per cent of Fijians are trapped in a cycle where their income does not meet their expenses, while 46 per cent say their income only matches their spending, leaving little or nothing to save.

Less than half of respondents reported saving money during the past year, and 61 per cent said they could cover living expenses for one month or less if they lost their main source of income.

Almost half (47 per cent) said they would need to borrow money from family or friends if faced with an unexpected financial emergency.

The findings suggest that while Fiji has made significant strides in expanding access to financial services and digital finance, improving household financial resilience and encouraging long-term savings remain major challenges.

item.title: Bushfire suspected after vacant Momi structure destroyed
item.description: The National Fire Authority is warning the public about the growing threat of bushfires after a vacant structure was destroyed in a fire at Momi Gun Side in Nadi on Tuesday evening. The Nadi Fire Station received a report of the fire at about 6.06pm and immediately dispatched two fire trucks with 12 firefighters, including two off-duty officers.
item.content:encoded:
The National Fire Authority is warning the public about the growing threat of bushfires after a vacant structure was destroyed in a fire at Momi Gun Side in Nadi on Tuesday evening.

The Nadi Fire Station received a report of the fire at about 6.06pm and immediately dispatched two fire trucks with 12 firefighters, including two off-duty officers.

Firefighters arrived at the scene at about 6.38pm to find the blaze had already reached the decay stage of combustion. The vacant structure, built from partial concrete, corrugated iron and timber, had collapsed after being completely destroyed.

The NFA said poor road conditions and the remote hillside location prevented fire appliances from reaching the structure directly, forcing firefighters to park about 120 metres away and proceed on foot.

No one was present when crews arrived, and the owner of the property could not be identified. The structure, measuring about 14 feet by 18 feet, appeared to have been unoccupied for a long period.

The building sustained 100 per cent fire damage, although the value of the loss has not been determined.

Preliminary observations suggest the fire may have started from a nearby bushfire before spreading to the structure, but the exact cause remains under investigation.

NFA chief executive Puamau Sowane said the incident demonstrated how rapidly bushfires could spread to nearby buildings.

“This incident is a concern because it demonstrates how quickly a bushfire can spread from vegetation to a nearby structure, resulting in significant property loss. While this particular building was vacant, the same circumstances could easily put occupied homes, neighbouring properties and communities at risk.”

Mr Sowane urged the public to exercise caution during the current dry and windy conditions.

“With dry and windy conditions, a fire that may initially appear small can quickly become difficult to control. We are therefore urging everyone to be extremely careful and responsible when dealing with fire, particularly in areas surrounded by dry vegetation.”

He also called on property owners to maintain vacant properties by clearing surrounding vegetation to reduce fire risks.

The NFA reminded the public to report any fire threatening lives or property by calling 910, and urged communities to remain vigilant during the current dry spell.

item.title: Road death toll rises to 31 after Navua crash claims two lives
item.description: Fiji’s road death toll has climbed to 31 after two elderly people were killed in a three-vehicle collision in Navua on Wednesday afternoon, prompting renewed calls from police for all road users to take greater responsibility for road safety. The victims, a 70-year-old man and a 67-year-old woman, died after the vehicle they were travelling in allegedly crossed onto the opposite lane, resulting in
item.content:encoded:
Fiji’s road death toll has climbed to 31 after two elderly people were killed in a three-vehicle collision in Navua on Wednesday afternoon, prompting renewed calls from police for all road users to take greater responsibility for road safety.

The victims, a 70-year-old man and a 67-year-old woman, died after the vehicle they were travelling in allegedly crossed onto the opposite lane, resulting in a multiple-vehicle crash.

Police said four people travelling in the other two vehicles sustained injuries but were treated at Navua Hospital and later discharged.

The bodies of the deceased have been taken to the Colonial War Memorial Hospital, where post-mortem examinations will be carried out.

The latest fatalities bring Fiji’s national road death toll to 31, down from 39 recorded during the same period last year.

Despite the year-on-year decline, police say every road death is preventable and are urging motorists and all road users to adopt a stronger sense of personal responsibility.

Police stressed that road safety should not be viewed as the sole responsibility of law enforcement agencies, saying everyone has a role to play in reducing crashes and saving lives.

Figures for the first six months of 2026 show speeding remains the leading cause of fatal road crashes in Fiji. Other contributing factors include careless driving, drink driving, pedestrians at fault, improper overtaking, and driver fatigue.

Authorities are again reminding drivers to obey speed limits, avoid taking unnecessary risks, remain alert behind the wheel and ensure their decisions on the road do not put the lives of others in danger.

item.title: People First rejects corruption claims over party launch
item.description: The People First Party has strongly denied allegations circulating on social media that its official launch was tainted by corruption, describing the claims as false, malicious and aimed at damaging the party’s reputation. In a statement posted on its official social media platforms, the party said allegations circulated on social media and other platforms were “baseless” and intended to undermine
item.content:encoded:
The People First Party has strongly denied allegations circulating on social media that its official launch was tainted by corruption, describing the claims as false, malicious and aimed at damaging the party’s reputation.

In a statement posted on its official social media platforms, the party said allegations circulated on social media and other platforms were “baseless” and intended to undermine the integrity of the newly formed political movement.

“These assertions are not only untrue but are a deliberate attempt to undermine the integrity and foundational principles of our nascent political movement,” said the party,

The party also rejected claims that individuals making the allegations had any authority within the organisation, saying they were not members of its Board of Governors.

“The individuals propagating these false narratives are in no way affiliated with or members of the People First Party’s Board of Governors. The Board of Governors is the sole authoritative body responsible for all strategic decisions, including the planning and execution of the party’s official launch.”

Addressing questions over the funding of its launch at Korovuto College, the party said the event was financed entirely through contributions from members of its Board of Governors.

“The launch event held at Korovuto College was made possible through the monthly financial contributions of our dedicated Board of Governors. These contributions were made with full transparency and in adherence to all relevant regulations, demonstrating our commitment to ethical practices from the outset.”

The party said transparency, accountability and integrity remained central to its operations and condemned what it described as attempts to spread misinformation.

“People First Party stands for transparency, accountability, and integrity. We condemn any attempts to spread misinformation and assure the public that our operations are conducted with the highest standards of ethical conduct.”

The party urged the public to rely on its official communication channels for accurate information and disregard what it described as malicious claims.

“We urge the public to disregard these malicious and unfounded claims, which are designed to sow discord and distrust. The People First Party remains steadfast in its mission to serve the Fijian people with honesty and dedication.”

The allegations referred to by the party have not been independently verified. The statement represents the People First Party’s response to claims circulating on social media.

item.title: People’s Alliance calls for party unity ahead of General Election
item.description: The General Secretary of the People’s Alliance Party, Sila Balawa, has called on party members to unite as preparations intensify for the next General Election, saying internal divisions must be set aside to strengthen the party’s campaign. Mr Balawa said his immediate priority is ensuring the party is organised, united and election-ready, stressing that this is the time for members to rally behin
item.content:encoded:
The General Secretary of the People’s Alliance Party, Sila Balawa, has called on party members to unite as preparations intensify for the next General Election, saying internal divisions must be set aside to strengthen the party’s campaign.

Mr Balawa said his immediate priority is ensuring the party is organised, united and election-ready, stressing that this is the time for members to rally behind a common purpose.

“If there is a time to be united, then this is it,” he said.

He urged members to put aside personal grievances and differences, saying unity would be critical to the party’s success at the polls.

“For those who may have differences or grumbles or whatever they have, they should put all that aside. We need to come together and fight as one single unit. Like the saying goes: united we stand, divided we fall.”

Mr Balawa said a united party would be better positioned to continue serving the people of Fiji and mount a strong campaign in the lead-up to the election.

He said the road to victory depended on members working together with a shared vision and common purpose.

“The road to victory is built on unity. When we stand together with one vision and one purpose, we are stronger, more resilient, and better placed to continue delivering for the people of Fiji.”

The People’s Alliance Party is expected to continue its organisational preparations and engagement with members nationwide as it gears up for the country’s next General Election.

item.title: Electoral Commission adopts fast-track rules for false statement appeals
item.description: The Electoral Commission has adopted new rules setting out an expedited process for reviewing decisions made by the Supervisor of Elections regarding the publication of false statements during elections. The Review of Decision of Supervisor Regarding Publication of False Statement Rules 2026, which came into effect on 29 July 2026, establish the procedures for appeals under Section 144A of the Ele
item.content:encoded:
The Electoral Commission has adopted new rules setting out an expedited process for reviewing decisions made by the Supervisor of Elections regarding the publication of false statements during elections.

The Review of Decision of Supervisor Regarding Publication of False Statement Rules 2026, which came into effect on 29 July 2026, establish the procedures for appeals under Section 144A of the Electoral Act 2014.

The rules require the Electoral Commission to determine any application for review within 24 hours of receiving a Notice of Review, in line with the requirements of the Electoral Act.

Under the rules, any person who has received a direction from the Supervisor of Elections under Section 144A(2) of the Act may apply for a review.

While no statutory deadline is prescribed for lodging a review, the Commission notes that the Interpretation Act requires applications to be filed without unreasonable delay, meaning they should be submitted as soon as practicable after the Supervisor’s decision.

The rules also establish strict timeframes for the exchange of documents between the parties. The Commission must provide the Supervisor with a copy of the application within 12 hours, while the Supervisor must respond within 12 hours of receiving it.

Political parties or other relevant persons may also be invited to participate as third parties, with similar accelerated filing requirements applying to any responses.

Given the statutory requirement to issue a decision within 24 hours, the Commission said all notices and responses must generally be filed within 18 hours of the initial application.

The rules also provide for the withdrawal of a review application through a prescribed form, with the Commission required to notify all parties of its decision on the withdrawal within 12 hours.

Importantly, the Commission has ruled out oral hearings for these matters.

It says no in-person hearing will be conducted because of the legal requirement to deliver a decision within 24 hours, with reviews instead determined through the expedited written process.

The new rules supplement the Electoral Commission’s broader Adjudication Procedure Rules 2026, providing specific forms, procedures and timelines for appeals relating to directions issued by the Supervisor of Elections over the publication of false statements.

item.title: Ro Teimumu highlights unfinished iTaukei reforms
item.description: THE Great Council of Chiefs (GCC) remains at the centre of unfinished iTaukei reforms, with Roko Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa saying the institution has yet to regain its “rightful position” under Fiji’s Constitution. Speaking during an interview after the launch of the celebrating women in Parliament booklet earlier this week, Ro Teimumu said despite progress made by the Coalition Government in re
item.content:encoded:
THE Great Council of Chiefs (GCC) remains at the centre of unfinished iTaukei reforms, with Roko Tui Dreketi Ro Teimumu Kepa saying the institution has yet to regain its “rightful position” under Fiji’s Constitution.

Speaking during an interview after the launch of the celebrating women in Parliament booklet earlier this week, Ro Teimumu said despite progress made by the Coalition Government in returning some land to traditional landowners, key reforms affecting iTaukei rights and institutions remained unresolved.

“To bring back the Great Council of Chiefs into its proper legislation, to enact it and to give autonomy,” she said.

She said the GCC’s restoration was not only about the institution itself, but also about recognising its historical role and contribution to Fiji’s governance.

“The FijiFirst Government decided that the way to do away with iTaukei rights to their resources was to chop from the top and that is why they targeted the Great Council of Chiefs.”

Ro Teimumu acknowledged that the Coalition Government had taken steps to address some of the concerns raised by iTaukei communities but said many issues could not be resolved within one term.

“What I’m talking about is the i qoliqoli, the land, the common name, and Bose Levu Vakaturaga.

“You cannot address everything in four years.”

She said the future of iTaukei institutions depended on continued efforts to ensure they had an effective role in Fiji’s development and decision-making.
